positions.text: Engl, Riedl, and Weber provide direct evidence for the identification logic and an important boundary on it. Their laboratory study keeps the public-goods game structure constant across treatments, varies whether and how an enforcement institution applies, and measures effects relative to a no-institution baseline. This design permits causal statements about the institutional treatment. It supports Kaal's premise that a fixed task environment can isolate an institutional contribution. The qualification is material. Engl, Riedl, and Weber use controlled treatment contrasts. Kaal's claim describes a sequential stage arc. Keeping the population, task distribution, and harness fixed does not by itself remove period, learning, order, or carryover effects. The external evidence therefore supports the controlled-comparison principle, but it does not validate the exact stage sequence or the later inferences attributed to it.

sourceEvidencePassages.text: Groups play two identical public good games. We vary whether, for only one game, there is an institution enforcing cooperation and vary also whether the institution is imposed exogenously or arises endogenously through voting.

In a baseline “no institution” treatment, behavior is not governed by any enforcement mechanism in either game. That is, subjects can freely choose their contribution to the public goods and free-riding in both games is a dominant strategy for narrowly selfish agents. In the other two treatments, one of the two games is monitored by an institution (“PGG Rule”), while the other is not (“PGG No Rule”).
Both are measured relative to contributions observed in the “no institution” treatment.
We use a linear public goods game as our workhorse, whose basic structure is constant across all parts and treatments.
